chapter: Learning violin and banjo in New Orleans
title: Father teaches him guitar chords and arranges violin lessons with Dave Perkins
summary: His father tests his sons with chord shapes, teaches Emanuel guitar changes, decides he should play violin, and buys a viola for $10 so he can study with his friend Dave Perkins.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: From listening to brass bands in Donovanville, you know. Oh, I see. Because they were strictly readers, you know. But Claiborne Williams did have an orchestra band, but I mean, by me being a kid, I didn't really get a chance to go out there then, you see. Yeah. Yeah. So we... She lived up there on Birdhead and Oak. Like I said, all the bands used to stop there. And I don't know, I forgot the time behind there. We moved on Ramport Street between 6th and Washington. And I went to a school called the Holy Ghost School, which is still up there. And I remember one time, my daddy took the streets, my oldest brother Pete, and my next brother Joe. And before I get to that, he used to always find me plucking around with his guitar. You know, he had his guitar he kept there, and I'd be fooling around like a kid, and I couldn't make a card. I'd just be strumming and trying to find a note, you know. So I remember he took one day, he took my oldest brother Pete, and my brother Joe and myself, he said, I'm going to show you all a card. He said, I want you to see who's going to grasp the idea the fastest. So he'd show them a card, and then he'd give it to Pete, then he'd give it to Joe, and then he'd give it to me. And I'd take the card, and then he'd bring it back to them, and he found out that they couldn't catch the eye of holding the card. But I could, it seemed like I could remember what he showed me, see. And he took another card and showed them. Well, it seemed like he was testing to see which one would really want to learn how to play music, you see. So then he taught me, I remember, after he taught me how to play three changes, I remember in the key of G. That was the G chord, the D7, and the C chord. Then he took me to the key of C, and he taught me the C chord, the F, and the G7, those simple changes. And after I learned that, he saw why I could play that pretty well. And I remember there was a song out at that time called Go Feather Your Nest. And he showed me how to play the chords on that. So I said, well, he said, well, it looked like he said, but I don't want you to play no guitar. He said, I want you to play violin. So I said, okay, Paul, I think I learned that. So he said, I've already talked to Dave Poick, and he says, he's willing to take it. He said, I wouldn't want nobody else to teach you but him, because we were good friends from way back. He says, I want him to teach you. He said, now, you already, which I did already have my little job. I used to work, and I remember I was waking, but 75 cents a week. I was waking on Coliseum at 7. Yeah, Coliseum at 7. I was waking after school, going up there doing yard boy, and cleaning up the yard in the evening. And then I'd do the little butler work, serve the people, you know, and then help the cook, clean up the kitchen, and come on back. I'd get back about 7 or 8 o'clock at night and study my lesson and then go to base, you know. Well, after that, well, when he took me to Dave Poick, well, he had a fellow, my dad was working at the Masonic Temple, the old Masonic Temple, and the fellow down there,
seemed like he had this all playing out, what he wanted me to play.

White Father had a violin he'd been talking to that one, and after he finally talked to this man that he had a son that wanted to learn violin, but he didn't have no big money to pay for no violin, but he wanted to get a good violin. So this white gentleman must have told him about he has a violin there, and he would sell it to read him a price. And I think my dad had bought that violin for $10, and it was a real good violin. I think that violin must have worth about $50 at that time. And, you know, I should be fooled with that. I was running on my dad, he had a viola, that's what it was. A viola was just larger than a violin. That's what I took lesson on that from Dave Poick.
